title: PhD Candidate in Hydroinformatics at IHE Delft: Uncertainty-Aware Optimisation for Robust Water Distribution System Operation
summary: Are you a Master’s graduate with a strong background in hydroinformatics, water engineering, civil or environmental engineering, applied mathematics, operations research, or computer science? Are you interested in artificial intelligence, optimisation, hydraulic modelling, uncertainty analysis, digital twins, and intelligent water systems? The IHE Delft Institute for Water Education is offering an exciting PhD Candidate position in Hydroinformatics as part of the Horizon Europe Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Doctoral Network i3WaterS – Intelligent, Innovative and Integrative Water Systems . This four-year doctoral research opportunity is designed for an ambitious researcher who wants to contribute to the future of intelligent, resilient, sustainable, and data-driven drinking-water distribution systems. The selected candidate will be based in Delft, the Netherlands , and will work within IHE Delft’s Hydroinformatics and Socio-Technical Innovation Department . The research will focus specifically on developing uncertainty-aware optimisation approaches that can help water utilities make better operational decisions when hydraulic models, operational data, water demand, and other inputs are uncertain. The position combines academic research, advanced computational methods, artificial intelligence, optimisation, water-system modelling, international collaboration, and practical engagement with water utilities. Opportunity Overview The PhD candidate will undertake research within the Horizon Europe-funded i3WaterS Doctoral Network , which brings together universities, research institutions, technology developers, and water utilities. The broader i3WaterS network will train 15 Doctoral Candidates in developing advanced approaches for intelligent water systems. The programme integrates: Monitoring data Expert knowledge Hydraulic models Water-quality models Digital twins Optimisation Artificial intelligence Machine learning Decision-support systems Uncertainty analysis Data-driven modelling The goal is to develop innovative approaches that can help drinking-water distribution systems become more intelligent, resilient, efficient, and sustainable. For this particular PhD project, the successful candidate will investigate how uncertainty can be explicitly incorporated into operational optimisation. PhD Research Topic Uncertainty-Aware Optimisation for Robust Water Distribution System Operation Water distribution systems are complex infrastructure networks. Their operation depends on many variables, including water demand, hydraulic conditions, network characteristics, operational decisions, and information obtained from monitoring systems. However, these variables are not always known with complete certainty. Hydraulic models may contain uncertainties, operational data may be incomplete or inaccurate, and water demand can fluctuate significantly. Consequently, an operational decision that appears optimal under one set of assumptions may not perform as expected when actual conditions differ. This PhD research will address this challenge by developing uncertainty-aware, model-based, multi-objective optimisation methodologies for drinking-water distribution systems. The research will explicitly account for uncertainty in hydraulic models and operational data and investigate how different sources of uncertainty influence operational decisions. An important part of the research will involve identifying which uncertainties are significant enough to justify further investigation or additional information gathering. The project will therefore make use of Value of Information (VoI) concepts to determine which uncertainty sources are worth resolving and which may not materially affect decisions. The ultimate goal is to advance computational methods that enable robust and potentially real-time operational optimisation for water distribution systems. Main Research Objectives The successful PhD candidate will be expected to contribute to several major research objectives. 1. Identify Important Sources of Uncertainty The research will develop methodologies and reproducible computational tools for determining which uncertainty sources have a meaningful impact on operational decisions. Not every uncertainty within a water distribution system will necessarily need to be resolved. The candidate will therefore investigate how uncertainties can be assessed and prioritised, including through Value of Information approaches. This can help water utilities focus their resources on collecting, improving, or resolving information that has the greatest influence on decision-making. 2. Develop Robust Optimisation Methods The project will develop methods for optimising water-distribution-system operations while accounting for uncertain inputs. Rather than assuming that all model parameters and operational conditions are perfectly known, the research will investigate optimisation approaches capable of producing decisions that remain effective under uncertainty. This will involve robust and potentially stochastic multi-objective optimisation approaches. 3. Develop Reproducible Code An important expected outcome of the PhD will be the development of reproducible research methodologies and software. The candidate is expected to produce: Reproducible code for identifying influential uncertainty sources Computational approaches for uncertainty-aware decision-making Code for robust optimisation of water distribution system operations Methods that can potentially support real-time operational decision-making Reproducibility will be important because the resulting methodologies should be useful for future research and potentially transferable to practical water-management applications. 4. Validate the Research Using a Real Utility Case The research will not remain purely theoretical. The developed methodologies will be validated using a real water utility case . The candidate will assess how the proposed methods perform under realistic operational conditions and evaluate their potential benefits and limitations. The validation will include an assessment of: Operational performance improvements Robustness of decisions Practical applicability Limitations of the proposed methods Effects of uncertainty on operational outcomes This real-world component provides an opportunity for the doctoral research to connect advanced computational research with practical water-utility challenges. Expected Results of the PhD The project identifies three major expected outcomes. Expected Result 1: Uncertainty Identification Methodology The candidate will develop a methodology and reproducible code capable of identifying uncertainty sources that materially affect operational decisions. Expected Result 2: Robust Optimisation Methodology The candidate will develop a methodology and associated code for robust optimisation of water-distribution-system operations under uncertain inputs. Expected Result 3: Real-World Validation The developed research will be tested using a real utility case, with an assessment of performance improvements and limitations. Together, these outputs are expected to contribute to more reliable and intelligent operational decision-making within drinking-water distribution systems. Host Institution: IHE Delft Institute for Water Education The selected candidate will be hosted by the Hydroinformatics and Socio-Technical Innovation Department at IHE Delft in Delft, Netherlands. IHE Delft is an international institution specialising in water education, research, and capacity development. The doctoral researcher will work within an interdisciplinary environment connecting water engineering, hydroinformatics, data science, artificial intelligence, modelling, optimisation, and socio-technical innovation. The position provides an opportunity to conduct doctoral research while collaborating with academic researchers, water-sector professionals, technology developers, and other doctoral researchers within the i3WaterS network. PhD Supervisory Team The doctoral candidate will benefit from a supervisory team involving academic and industry expertise. Main Supervisor: Associate Professor Leonardo Alfonso Associate Professor Leonardo Alfonso of IHE Delft will serve as the main supervisor. Co-Supervisor: Dr Oscar Coronado Hernandez Dr Oscar Coronado Hernandez from the University of Cartagena will serve as co-supervisor. Industrial Mentor: Dr Claudia Quintiliani Dr Claudia Quintiliani from Brabant Water will act as the industrial mentor. This combination of academic and industry supervision is particularly relevant because the research is intended to address both methodological research questions and practical water-utility challenges. International Training and Mobility One of the major advantages of this opportunity is participation in the i3WaterS International Doctoral School . The Doctoral School is organised across six chapters in: Barcelona Dublin Bordeaux Delft Brussels Newcastle The international training programme is designed to provide doctoral researchers with technical, research, professional, and transferable skills. Training areas include: Artificial intelligence and machine learning Explainable AI Trustworthy AI Knowledge representation Multi-agent systems Intelligent decision-support systems Digital twins Smart water systems Innovation Entrepreneurship Scientific communication Transferable professional skills This means the successful candidate will not only work on their individual PhD research but will also participate in an international training environment with researchers from different institutions and countries. International Secondments The doctoral programme includes international secondments that will provide additional practical and research experience. University of Cartagena Secondment A three-month secondment at the University of Cartagena (UC) is planned from project month 21. The secondment will focus on: Water-demand forecasting Optimal water-system operation Specialised training Research collaboration The candidate will also collaborate with Aguas de Cartagena (AC) during this period. This secondment will provide exposure to water-demand forecasting and operational challenges in a different geographical and institutional context. Cetaqua Secondment A second secondment lasting two months is planned at Cetaqua (CET) from project month 34. The purpose of this secondment will be to: Test the research findings Validate the developed approaches Collaborate with specialists Assess the practical applicability of the research The timing of either secondment may be adjusted in consultation with the supervisory team and host organisations. Responsibilities of the PhD Candidate The successful applicant will have a broad range of academic, research, technical, and collaborative responsibilities. Research and Method Development The candidate will: Plan and develop the research methodology. Implement the methods and tools identified in the project objectives. Follow developments in state-of-the-art decision-making under uncertainty. Investigate robust multi-objective optimisation approaches. Apply these approaches to drinking-water distribution systems. Develop computational methods for operational decision-making. Project Participation The researcher will also contribute to the wider i3WaterS project by participating in: Project deliverables Technical reports Research meetings Network-wide activities Collaborative research activities Academic Publications The candidate will be expected to disseminate research findings through academic channels. This includes: Publishing research in peer-reviewed journals Presenting findings at national conferences Presenting at international conferences Participating in symposia Communicating research results to academic and professional audiences International Collaboration The candidate will actively participate in: The International Doctoral School International secondments Collaborative research activities Academic partnerships Non-academic partner activities MSc Thesis Support Where appropriate, the doctoral candidate may also support or mentor MSc thesis projects related to the doctoral research. PhD Thesis The ultimate responsibility will be to prepare and successfully defend a doctoral thesis within the appointment period. Required Qualifications Applicants must meet the academic and technical requirements of the position. Master s Degree Applicants must hold a Master s degree with strong academic results in one of the following fields: Hydroinformatics Civil engineering Environmental engineering Water engineering Applied mathematics Operations research Computer science A closely related field Applicants whose Master s degree is in another discipline may potentially be considered if their academic and technical background is closely aligned with the requirements of the research project. Hydraulics and Hydraulic Modelling Applicants should have strong knowledge of: Hydraulics Hydraulic modelling Drinking-water distribution systems This is a particularly important requirement because the PhD focuses directly on the optimisation and operation of water-distribution networks. Candidates should therefore be comfortable working with the technical principles behind water-distribution-system modelling. Optimisation Applicants should have knowledge of optimisation. Experience with multi-objective optimisation is particularly desirable. Knowledge or interest in the following areas will also be valuable: Robust optimisation Stochastic optimisation Decision-making under uncertainty Mathematical optimisation Computational optimisation Programming Applicants are expected to have programming experience in Python . Experience with optimisation libraries is highly desirable. Knowledge of water-network modelling software is also considered highly desirable. Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Experience in the following areas is an advantage: Data science Machine learning Uncertainty quantification Value of Information methods Artificial intelligence Data-driven modelling These skills can strengthen an applicant s profile, particularly because the wider i3WaterS network focuses on intelligent and AI-enabled water systems. English Language Requirements Applicants must demonstrate proficiency in written and spoken English . The position also requires the ability to independently write academic texts in English. This is important because the candidate will be expected to produce: Research papers Technical reports PhD research documentation Conference presentations The doctoral thesis Other academic and project-related materials Personal and Professional Competencies In addition to academic qualifications, IHE Delft is looking for a candidate with a collaborative and proactive attitude. The ideal candidate should demonstrate: Ability to conduct independent research Proactive working style Strong collaboration skills Interest in multidisciplinary research Ability to work in multicultural environments Willingness to collaborate with academic and non-academic partners Strong written communication Strong analytical thinking Capacity to learn advanced technical methods Because the project involves multiple universities, research institutions, technology developers, and water utilities, the ability to work effectively with people from different professional and cultural backgrounds will be important. MSCA Doctoral Network Eligibility In addition to the academic requirements, applicants must satisfy the eligibility conditions applicable to Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Networks . You Must Not Already Hold a Doctoral Degree At the date of recruitment, the applicant must be a Doctoral Candidate . The candidate must not already hold a doctoral degree and must not have defended a doctoral thesis. This means the position is intended for researchers who are entering or undertaking their doctoral research rather than individuals who have already completed a PhD. MSCA Mobility Rule The MSCA mobility rule also applies. During the 36 months immediately before the recruitment date , the applicant must not have: Resided in the Netherlands for more than 12 months; or Carried out their main activity in the Netherlands for more than 12 months. Main activity includes activities such as work or studies. Certain periods are excluded from this calculation, including: Compulsory national service Time spent obtaining refugee status under the Geneva Convention Applicants should carefully verify their personal mobility history before applying because satisfying the MSCA mobility rule is an essential eligibility condition. Employment Duration This is a 48-month, four-year PhD position . The position is based on a working schedule of 38 hours per week . The expectation is that the candidate will complete and successfully defend the PhD thesis within the four-year appointment period. Initial Contract The initial employment contract will be for 18 months . During the first year, a go/no-go decision will be made. This decision will be based on a detailed PhD research proposal developed by the candidate. Following this assessment, the contract may be extended if the candidate successfully meets the required expectations. Salary and Employment Conditions Employment at IHE Delft will be according to the Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Universities , under scale P . The appointment also includes entry into the Netherlands Civil Service Pension Fund (ABP) . The final remuneration package will be determined according to: IHE Delft employment conditions Applicable MSCA Doctoral Network allowances Applicants should therefore understand that the position is not simply an academic study opportunity but a formal employment-based doctoral appointment with associated employment conditions. Expected Start Date The expected contract starting date is: 1 January 2027 Applicants should be prepared to commence the doctoral appointment around this date if selected. Application Deadline The application deadline is: 20 September 2026 at 23:59 CEST (Brussels time) Applicants are strongly encouraged to submit their applications before the deadline rather than waiting until the final hours. title: Scaling Climate Finance: Free 7-Hour UN Online Course on Climate Finance, Public Investment and Private Capital
summary: The Scaling Climate Finance e-course is a self-paced online learning opportunity designed to strengthen participants’ knowledge and understanding of the climate finance system and the different ways financial resources can be mobilised to support climate action. The course responds to a growing global need for greater investment in climate change mitigation and adaptation. As governments, businesses, financial institutions, civil society organizations and other stakeholders face increasing pressure to respond to climate impacts, understanding how climate finance works has become increasingly important. Offered through the UN CC platform , the course explores public and private sources of climate finance, financing instruments and mechanisms, public investment management, innovative approaches to mobilising capital, and the importance of gender equality and social inclusion in climate finance decision-making. The course takes approximately 7 hours to complete , is self-paced , and is available in English . Participants who successfully complete the required quizzes can obtain a digital certificate of completion for a USD 30 certification fee . About the Scaling Climate Finance E-Course Climate change requires significant financial resources. Countries need investment not only to reduce greenhouse gas emissions but also to strengthen resilience and adapt to the effects of a changing climate. The Scaling Climate Finance e-course has been developed to help participants better understand this financial landscape and identify opportunities for mobilising and using climate finance more effectively. According to the course description, opportunities to mobilise finance for climate action are expanding through smarter use of public finance, the unlocking of new pools of private capital, and the development of innovative financing channels. However, the climate finance system can be complex. There are numerous financial sources, instruments, actors and mechanisms involved, making it difficult for professionals and other stakeholders to determine how different elements fit together. The course therefore aims to provide participants with the knowledge, motivation and practical methods needed to understand and contribute to efforts to scale climate finance. Why Climate Finance Matters The climate crisis is already affecting communities, economies and societies around the world. Addressing these impacts requires urgent action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions while simultaneously building resilience to climate-related risks. Finance is a fundamental enabler of this action. The course notes that responding effectively to climate change requires trillions of dollars in investment globally each year, while only a fraction of the required amount is currently being channelled toward climate action. This creates both a major challenge and an important opportunity. On one hand, there is a significant financing gap that must be addressed. On the other hand, climate finance is expanding, with new financing avenues, mechanisms and sources emerging each year. The course highlights the increasing diversity of climate finance channels and innovations in how financial resources can be coordinated and supplied. These developments mean that stakeholders across the public and private sectors can play an important role in helping countries mobilise more finance for climate action. What Does the Scaling Climate Finance Course Cover? The course provides a broad introduction to the climate finance system and examines how different stakeholders, financial mechanisms and investment approaches can contribute to climate action. By completing the course, participants are expected to develop an understanding of several important areas. 1. Climate Finance Sources, Instruments and Mechanisms Participants will learn to identify key sources of climate finance and understand the different instruments and mechanisms used to channel financial resources toward climate action. The course specifically examines how these different elements interact to support both: Climate change mitigation; and Climate change adaptation. This understanding can help participants recognize the different ways climate-related projects and programmes can be financed. 2. Roles of Different Climate Finance Actors Climate finance involves a wide range of stakeholders, each with different responsibilities and roles. The course explores the importance of different actors within the climate finance system and helps participants understand how these stakeholders can contribute to mobilising and effectively using climate finance. This is particularly relevant to professionals working in government, financial institutions, the private sector, civil society and other organizations involved in climate-related decision-making. 3. Coordinating Public Climate Finance The course examines measures, tools and approaches that can be used to coordinate public climate finance more efficiently and effectively. For governments and public-sector institutions, this knowledge can be particularly valuable because effective coordination is essential when planning, budgeting and implementing climate-related investments. Participants can therefore gain insights into how public resources can be better aligned with national climate priorities. 4. Private and Innovative Climate Finance The course also explores innovative sources, mechanisms and financial instruments that can provide access to new pools of capital for climate action. Particular attention is given to opportunities to mobilise financing from the private sector. As climate investment needs continue to grow, understanding how public and private finance can complement one another is increasingly important for policymakers, financial professionals, investors and climate practitioners. 5. Gender Equality and Social Inclusion in Climate Finance An important feature of the course is its gender equality and social inclusion (GESI) lens . Participants will learn how applying a gender equality and social inclusion perspective to climate finance can help ensure that investments reach people and communities that are particularly at risk or vulnerable to climate impacts. The course uses case studies, examples and stories to demonstrate how gender equality and social inclusion can be incorporated into: Climate finance planning; Budgeting; Investment decisions; Climate change mitigation; and Climate change adaptation. This approach recognizes that climate change does not affect all people and communities in the same way and that climate finance decisions can have different consequences for different groups. Public Investment Management and Climate Finance Another major area covered by the course is Public Investment Management (PIM) . Participants will learn how Public Investment Management operates within the broader Public Finance Management (PFM) system. The course also examines where handovers within these systems can weaken the use of evidence. Understanding this relationship can be important for professionals involved in government planning, budgeting, investment decisions and the implementation of climate-related projects. Effective public investment systems can help governments ensure that limited financial resources are directed toward investments capable of delivering meaningful climate and development outcomes. Course Structure The Scaling Climate Finance e-course is organized into five modules followed by a final quiz . Each module combines different learning approaches, including short introductory videos, interactive lessons, case studies and exercises. Module 1: What is Climate Finance? The first module introduces participants to the concept of climate finance and provides a foundation for understanding the broader climate finance system. Participants begin by exploring the sources, instruments and mechanisms through which finance can support climate action. Module 2: Making Public Finance Go Further for Climate Action The second module focuses on how public finance can be used more effectively to support climate objectives. It examines approaches that can help governments coordinate and maximize the impact of public financial resources dedicated to climate action. Module 3: Mobilising Private and Innovative Climate Finance The third module turns attention to private-sector investment and innovative financing approaches. Participants explore ways of accessing new pools of capital and understand how innovative climate finance mechanisms can contribute to addressing the significant financing requirements associated with climate action. Module 4: Financing a Climate Change Plan The fourth module focuses on financing climate change plans. This section is particularly relevant to professionals involved in climate policy, planning, budgeting and investment because financing is an essential component of translating climate strategies and plans into practical action. Module 5: Scaling Climate-Smart Public Investment Management The fifth module examines how public investment management can be strengthened and scaled in ways that support climate-smart investment. It connects Public Investment Management with the wider Public Finance Management system and considers how the quality of decision-making and evidence can influence climate-related investments. Final Quiz After completing the five modules, participants undertake a final quiz as part of the course completion requirements. Who Should Take the Scaling Climate Finance Course? The course is designed for a broad audience because climate finance involves stakeholders across government, financial markets, civil society and the wider public. Although many of the tools, instruments and approaches are presented from a government and public-sector perspective, the course is intended to be relevant to several categories of participants. Government and Public-Sector Professionals The course is particularly relevant to policy, planning and technical personnel responsible for managing or mobilising climate finance at national and sub-national levels. This includes individuals working in: Central finance ministries; Planning ministries; Relevant line ministries; Sub-national governments; and Parliaments. These professionals can benefit from understanding how climate finance can be coordinated and mobilised to support national and sub-national climate priorities. Quasi-Governmental Organizations The course is also relevant to individuals working in organizations such as: State or central banks; State-owned enterprises; Parastatals; Supreme audit institutions; and Securities or exchange commissions. Such organizations can play significant roles in financial governance, investment, regulation, oversight and the broader climate finance system. Private-Sector Stakeholders Private-sector stakeholders and market facilitators can also benefit from the course. The programme is relevant to individuals and organizations that influence or enable climate-aligned investments and who want to better understand the mechanisms through which private capital can contribute to climate action. NGOs and Civil Society Organizations Practitioners working in non-governmental organizations and civil society groups are another important target audience. Understanding climate finance can help organizations engaged in climate advocacy, policy engagement, development programmes and accountability efforts better understand how climate resources are generated, allocated and used. Think Tanks and Education Institutions The course can also be useful for practitioners from regional and national think tanks as well as education and training institutions working on climate-related issues. Researchers, educators and policy analysts can use the knowledge gained through the course to strengthen their understanding of climate finance and its relationship with climate policy and investment. Interested Citizens The opportunity is not limited to professionals. Citizens who want to understand how finance enables climate action can also take the course. The knowledge can help individuals better understand the financial dimensions of climate change and hold relevant institutions and decision-makers accountable. Is the Course Available Worldwide? The course information indicates that while many of its case studies are drawn from the Asia-Pacific region , the tools, instruments and approaches covered can be relevant and applicable to individuals from all regions of the world . Therefore, the provided course information does not restrict participation to a particular country, nationality, race or continent. It is particularly useful for people whose professional or academic interests relate to climate finance, climate policy, public finance, investment, sustainable development or climate action, regardless of their geographic location. Course Duration and Learning Format The Scaling Climate Finance programme is designed as a 7-hour self-paced e-learning course . The self-paced format means participants can work through the learning materials according to their own schedule rather than attending a fixed live classroom programme. The course includes: Introductory videos; Interactive learning activities; Case studies; Exercises; Five learning modules; and A final quiz. The course is delivered in English . Digital Certificate of Completion Participants who successfully complete the course can qualify for a digital certificate of completion. To qualify for the certificate, participants must obtain a passing grade of at least 70% on all quizzes . There is an important assessment requirement: participants have up to three attempts per quiz . After successfully passing all quizzes, participants can obtain their digital certificate after paying the required USD 30 certification fee . Once payment has been completed, the certificate can be accessed and downloaded digitally. The certificate is designed to make it easier for participants to verify and share their achievement. It is important to distinguish between completing the learning opportunity and obtaining the digital certification: the course information specifically states that the digital certificate becomes available upon payment of the USD 30 fee after all quiz requirements have been successfully met. APPLY HERE Organizations Behind the Course The Scaling Climate Finance e-course is associated with several organizations working in climate finance, development and learning. United Nations Institute for Training and Research The United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) provides learning solutions to individuals, organizations and institutions. Its work focuses on enhancing global decision-making and supporting action at the country level. UNITAR s strategic framework is aligned with the 2030 Agenda , with the Sustainable Development Goals providing a guiding framework for its work. UNDP Asia-Pacific Climate Finance Network The course also involves the Asia-Pacific Climate Finance Network (CFN) , a peer-to-peer network and knowledge-management and technical-support facility managed by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) . The network assists Ministries of Finance, sector ministries, sub-national governments, private-sector stakeholders and development cooperation partners in identifying and scaling climate finance reforms across 18 countries in Asia and the Pacific . The Climate Finance Network is supported by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth Development Office (FCDO) for the period 2022–2028. The Government of Sweden also contributes to the network through the Governance of Climate Change Finance to Enhance Gender Equality initiative. Key Benefits of Taking the Course The Scaling Climate Finance course can provide several benefits to people working or interested in climate action and sustainable development. Gain a Better Understanding of Climate Finance Participants can develop a stronger understanding of how the climate finance system operates and how different financial sources, instruments and mechanisms interact. Understand Public and Private Financing The course covers both public finance and private-sector capital, giving learners a broader perspective on how different sources of funding can contribute to climate action. Learn About Innovative Financing Mechanisms Participants can explore innovative approaches for unlocking additional pools of capital and scaling climate finance. Strengthen Knowledge of Climate Investment The course introduces concepts related to Public Investment Management and its relationship with Public Finance Management, which can be valuable for professionals involved in government investment decisions. Incorporate Gender and Social Inclusion Learners can develop a better understanding of how climate finance can be designed and implemented with gender equality and social inclusion considerations. Learn at Your Own Pace Because the programme is self-paced and requires approximately seven hours, participants can fit the learning experience around their professional or personal schedules. Earn a Digital Certificate Participants who achieve at least 70% on all quizzes can qualify for a digital certificate of completion, subject to payment of the USD 30 certification fee. Apply Knowledge Across Different Regions Although the course uses many Asia-Pacific case studies, its tools, instruments and approaches are presented as being relevant to individuals from regions around the world. Who Can Benefit Most From This Opportunity? While the course is broadly accessible, it may be particularly valuable for people whose work or interests involve: Climate finance and climate investment. Public finance and government budgeting. Climate policy and planning. Sustainable development. Environmental policy. Public Investment Management. Financial-sector development. Private-sector climate investment. Climate change mitigation and adaptation. Gender-responsive climate action. Social inclusion. Civil society and climate advocacy. Research and policy analysis. Government accountability and oversight. It can therefore serve as a useful professional development resource for both specialists and people who are developing their knowledge of climate finance. Visit HERE for more information about the Free 7-Hour UN Online Course on Climate Finance. Eligibility and Geographic Scope The provided course information does not specify a particular academic degree, professional qualification, minimum age, nationality or race requirement . Instead, it describes a broad range of intended participants, including government officials, financial-sector stakeholders, private-sector actors, NGOs, civil society practitioners, think tanks, education and training institutions, and interested citizens. The course information also states that the approaches featured can be relevant to individuals from all regions around the world , even though many of the case studies come from the Asia-Pacific region. Consequently, prospective participants should not assume that the programme is restricted to Asia-Pacific nationals based solely on the regional focus of some of its examples. Application Deadline There is no application deadline stated in the provided course information . The opportunity is presented as a self-paced online course available through the UN CC platform. Prospective learners should nevertheless check the official course page for the latest enrolment and course-access information before beginning the programme. How the Course Can Support Climate Action Climate finance is not simply about raising money. It is also about ensuring that available financial resources are coordinated, directed and invested effectively. The Scaling Climate Finance course addresses this broader challenge by looking at the systems through which climate finance is mobilised and managed. For governments, this can involve improving the coordination of public finance and strengthening public investment management. For financial institutions and private-sector stakeholders, it can involve identifying opportunities to mobilise capital for climate-aligned investments. For civil society organizations and citizens, understanding climate finance can strengthen the ability to participate in discussions, advocate for effective resource allocation and hold institutions accountable. The course s focus on gender equality and social inclusion further emphasizes the importance of ensuring that climate investments benefit populations that may face greater vulnerability to climate change. Conclusion The Scaling Climate Finance e-course provides a comprehensive introduction to one of the most important components of global climate action: the mobilisation and effective use of financial resources. With approximately 7 hours of self-paced learning , the programme gives participants an opportunity to explore climate finance sources, financial instruments, public and private financing, innovative mechanisms, climate change planning, Public Investment Management, and gender equality and social inclusion. The course is particularly relevant to government officials, financial-sector professionals, private-sector stakeholders, NGOs, civil society organizations, researchers, think tanks, education institutions and citizens seeking to understand how finance can support climate action. Participants who successfully achieve at least 70% on all quizzes can qualify for a digital certificate of completion, with certification available after payment of the USD 30 fee . Learners have up to three attempts for each quiz. There is no specific application deadline stated in the available course information, and the course indicates that its approaches can be applicable to people from all regions of the world . For anyone seeking to strengthen their knowledge of climate finance, understand how public and private capital can be mobilised, or build a stronger foundation in climate-smart investment and financing, the Scaling Climate Finance e-course offers a structured opportunity to develop relevant knowledge and skills. title: UNA-NCA Graduate Fellows Program 2027: Develop Your UN Lens and Prepare for a Career in International Affairs
summary: The United Nations Association of the National Capital Area (UNA-NCA) Graduate Fellows Program (GFP) 2027 is offering graduate students in the Washington, DC, Maryland, and Northern Virginia region an opportunity to deepen their understanding of United Nations issues, policies, organizations, and global affairs while developing skills and professional connections relevant to UN-related careers. The program brings together graduate students, experienced faculty, foreign affairs professionals, and professionals connected to the United Nations system. Through weekly seminars, mentoring, career development activities, networking opportunities, and exposure to contemporary global issues, Fellows learn to examine international challenges through what the program describes as a “UN lens.” Applications for the 2027 Graduate Fellows Program are now open until October 4, 2026 . The program has a long history. Founded by UNA-NCA in 1991 , the Graduate Fellows Program has brought together UNA-NCA s resources with more than 500 students and 40 international public and nongovernmental organizations . For graduate students interested in international affairs, diplomacy, development, human rights, peacekeeping, sustainable development, migration, climate issues, or other UN-related fields, the program provides an opportunity to combine academic learning with professional development and exposure to the international affairs community in the Washington metropolitan area. About the UNA-NCA Graduate Fellows Program The United Nations Association of the National Capital Area works with more than 2,000 members, volunteers, and supporters in the greater Washington, DC, area. Its broader work focuses on: Building public knowledge about the United Nations Strengthening U.S.-UN relations Supporting the United Nations in achieving its goals Within this broader mission, the Graduate Fellows Program is designed specifically to help graduate students develop a stronger understanding of the United Nations and prepare for careers connected to international affairs and the UN system. The program combines academic seminars with professional development and mentoring. Rather than focusing exclusively on classroom learning, the GFP seeks to expose Fellows to the practical world of international affairs through its professional network and connections with the United Nations system. What Does “Developing Your UN Lens” Mean? A central idea behind the Graduate Fellows Program is learning to view global issues through a “UN lens.” This means examining contemporary international issues in relation to the United Nations, its organizations, policies, programs, and broader international system. Fellows have the opportunity to explore global challenges alongside: Like-minded graduate students Experienced faculty Foreign affairs professionals Prominent guest speakers Professionals connected to the UN system The program therefore encourages Fellows to go beyond simply studying international issues academically and consider how those issues are addressed within the broader United Nations system. Who Can Participate in the Graduate Fellows Program? The program is open to graduate students studying at universities within the DC-Maryland-Northern Virginia region . Applicants should be studying: International affairs Trade Development Another discipline related to the United Nations The program also welcomes certain applicants outside the traditional full-time graduate student category. Part-Time Students Part-time graduate students are welcome to apply. The program specifically encourages part-time students to consider the opportunity. Student Interns Student interns working in the DC area in fields relevant to the program may also apply. Young Professionals Young professionals working part-time in a related field are especially encouraged to apply. Students Studying Outside the DMV Graduate students who are not attending a university in the DMV region may also apply if they receive approval from the Graduate Fellows Program Director . The source also states that graduate students temporarily residing in the DMV region while attending a school outside the region may apply if they receive preliminary approval. International Students Are Encouraged to Apply One important feature of the program is that American citizenship is not required . The program explicitly encourages international students to apply. This means the Graduate Fellows Program is not limited to U.S. citizens. However, applicants must still meet the program s other eligibility requirements, including the requirement concerning UNA-NCA membership and the relevant graduate-study or professional background. UNA-NCA Membership Requirement Applicants must be current, active members of UNA-NCA to be considered. This is an important eligibility condition. The selection process considers the applicant s application, including their current and active UNA-NCA membership. Prospective applicants should therefore ensure that they satisfy the membership requirement before applying. Time Commitment for Fellows Selected Fellows are expected to commit approximately four hours per week to the Graduate Fellows Program. The expected commitment is divided into: Two hours: Weekly seminar Two hours: Seminar preparation, career strategy, and mentoring The program recognizes that graduate students may already have significant academic and professional responsibilities. Accordingly, the program faculty pay attention to the amount of time required for weekly assignments. This makes the structure designed to accommodate Fellows who may have a full course load as well as full-time or part-time professional commitments. Weekly Graduate Fellows Seminar The weekly seminar is one of the central components of the program. During the spring semester , Fellows participate in an in-person seminar every Friday. The seminars focus on pressing contemporary global issues and examine them through the program s “UN lens.” Fellows also have opportunities to learn from prominent guest speakers from across the United Nations system. This provides an opportunity to connect academic discussions with the practical work of international organizations and foreign affairs professionals. Major Topics Covered in the Weekly Seminars The Graduate Fellows Program covers a broad range of contemporary international issues. Thematic areas include: Economic Development and Economic Policy Fellows explore issues related to economic development and economic policy and consider their relevance to international development and the UN system. UN Budget and Finance The program examines issues related to the United Nations budget and financial structures. Gender Gender is another thematic area addressed through the program s global-issues discussions. Human Rights, Education, and Social Development Fellows examine questions surrounding human rights, education, and social development. Energy, Sustainable Development, and Climate Change The program also addresses major global challenges related to energy, sustainability, and climate change. Conflict Prevention, Conflict Resolution, and Peacekeeping Peace and security are important elements of the curriculum, including conflict prevention, conflict resolution, and peacekeeping. Refugees and Migration The program also explores international issues surrounding refugees and migration. United Nations Agenda 2030 and the Sustainable Development Goals The UN Agenda 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are also incorporated into the Graduate Fellows Program. Fellows are expected to complete a series of materials before each seminar. These may include: Readings Listening materials Viewing materials These preparatory assignments allow Fellows to arrive at seminars with background knowledge and engage meaningfully in discussions. The program recognizes that Fellows may already have demanding academic and professional schedules, and faculty therefore pay careful attention to the amount of time required for weekly assignments. Professional Development and Career Support The Graduate Fellows Program is not limited to academic seminars. A major component of the program is professional development . The program provides career support designed to help Fellows prepare for careers related to their interests. Professional development activities include: Career strategy sessions Resume preparation Resume review Mentor matching Connections with experienced professionals UNA-NCA uses its extensive professional network to arrange mentoring opportunities with seasoned professionals working in areas relevant to Fellows interests. This can help participants think more strategically about how their graduate education can translate into careers in international affairs and related fields. Mentoring Opportunities Mentoring is another important component of the Graduate Fellows Program. UNA-NCA facilitates mentor matching with experienced professionals operating in areas relevant to the Fellows interests. The purpose of mentoring is to provide Fellows with additional professional guidance as they consider their career paths. Through these interactions, Fellows can gain exposure to perspectives from professionals already working in relevant fields. Access to UNA-NCA s Professional Network A major strength of the program is UNA-NCA s professional network. The organization has relationships with: The United Nations system of agencies International public organizations Nongovernmental organizations Foreign affairs professionals Other professionals working in relevant fields According to the program description, this access to the UN system and its diverse professional relationships is a cornerstone of the Graduate Fellows Program s success. For students seeking to understand how international organizations operate and how careers in international affairs develop, this network can be particularly valuable. Young Professionals Program Opportunities Graduate Fellows also receive membership in the UNA-NCA Young Professionals Program . This includes invitations to networking events. The Young Professionals Program provides another opportunity for Fellows to interact with people working or developing careers in international affairs and related areas. However, Fellows have a specific participation requirement connected to completion of the Graduate Fellows Program.
